title: Suchness (section 17)
hook: "Tathagata" means suchness; there was nothing to receive from the past Buddha

segments.voice: Yesterday: despised and cleansed. Scorn borne by someone keeping the sutra wipes old wrongs away. Your line: cleansed by scorn. Did a small slight pass through you? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

Halfway through a long conversation, a good friend sometimes says: wait, ask me the first thing again. Not because they forgot. Because everything said since then has changed what the question means. Section seventeen of the Diamond Sutra does exactly that. Subhuti asks his opening question a second time, in nearly the same words: how should one who has set out on the path stand, go on, and hold the mind? The answer comes back with a new word at its center, and it's the name of the Buddha himself. Today: suchness.
screen: `ASK ME THE FIRST THING AGAIN.` → `THE SAME QUESTION, SECOND TIME.` → `A NEW WORD AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: First, the repeat. The Buddha answers much as he did at the start. Someone on this path should think: I will lead all beings to nirvana. And yet, once they are led, no being has been led. A bodhisattva who holds the idea of a self, he says, is not a bodhisattva. Then he goes further: there is no fixed thing called one who has set out. Second, the memory. The Buddha asks Subhuti about his own past. Long ago, under the earlier Buddha Dipankara, did he receive some thing that was the highest awakening? No, Subhuti says. Nothing. And the Buddha agrees. If there had been some thing to receive, he says, Dipankara would not have told him: in a future age, you will be a Buddha named Shakyamuni. It was because there was nothing to grasp that the prediction could be made. Third, the name. Why? Because, the sutra says, Tathagata, the title the Buddha uses for himself, is a name for suchness. Suchness means things just as they are, before we add our labels, our hopes, our stories about them. The Buddha's own name, in this sentence, points away from a person holding a prize and toward the plain way things are. Fourth, the everyday edge. Suchness isn't somewhere far off. It's the floor under your feet being exactly this floor. It's the rain being rain, before it's ruining anyone's plans. The sutra adds that the bodhisattva who says I will make the buddha-lands beautiful isn't truly one. Even good work, held as my project, slips away from suchness. That's this week, really. The sands of the Ganges, the ground made a shrine, the diamond that cuts, Subhuti's tears, the shoulders, the scorn: each one stripping a label off, so something can be seen as it is.
screen: `THE SAME ANSWER, NO ONE LED.` · `NOTHING RECEIVED FROM DIPANKARA.` · `TATHAGATA: A NAME FOR SUCHNESS.` · `THE FLOOR, JUST THIS FLOOR.` · then, large: `SUCHNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: see one thing just as it is. This time, let the one thing be the breath. Settle, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Feel one breath come in and go out. Notice the labels that arrive with it: too shallow, better, calmer now, am I doing this right. Let each one go by, like a car passing. Come back to the breath itself: cool at the nostrils, a rise in the belly, a pause, a fall. It doesn't need to be a good breath or a deep one. Just this breath, as it is, then the next. When a label returns, let it pass and feel again. The bell holds the time.
Suchness. Things just as they are. In section seventeen, the sutra says the name Tathagata itself means suchness. Today's word.
Your line: suchness. This week ends here. Today, once, catch yourself labeling something, and look at it again without the label. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: In Mahayana teaching, suchness (tathata) names reality as it is, without added concepts; meditators in some schools practice simply resting attention on what is present, without labeling it.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: under Dipankara, did I receive some thing that was the highest awakening? what do you say?
options: no, there was nothing to receive
fork.reveal: Subhuti says no, and the Buddha agrees: if there had been something to grasp, Dipankara couldn't have foretold it.

original.note: Sanskrit: suchness, things as they are; section 17 links it to the name Tathagata.

trapdoor: what you thought: Tathagata is just an honorific for the Buddha.
what it means: the sutra says the name means suchness, things just as they are.
what a scholar hears: the repeated question of section 2 answered again, with Dipankara's prediction possible only because nothing was attained.
